**“Duplicate” must be defined before choosing an algorithm.** Identical bytes, nearly identical wording, different photos of the same object, and two articles about the same event are different relationships. One embedding threshold cannot reliably serve every definition.

**Use stages matched to the definition.** Exact hashes cheaply identify byte-identical content. Shingle-based MinHash helps find substantial text overlap. SimHash approximates angular similarity of weighted features. Neural embeddings can find semantic resemblance even with different wording, but may incorrectly merge distinct claims on the same topic. [3](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/)

**Candidate generation is not final verification.** An approximate index should find likely pairs cheaply; a stricter comparison then decides whether they meet the duplicate definition. For video, temporal segment evidence matters: one shared thumbnail does not establish that two full videos are duplicates.

**Beware transitive clustering.** If A resembles B and B resembles C, A need not resemble C enough to merge. A chain of weak similarities can collapse many distinct documents into one cluster. Choose a clustering rule appropriate to the task and retain evidence for reversible merges.

Evaluate labeled pairs containing hard nonduplicates, edits, crops, and boilerplate. Track false merges separately from missed duplicates because their downstream costs differ. Store canonical IDs, versions, and deletion lineage so deduplication does not destroy provenance. A high pairwise similarity score is a useful signal, not an intrinsic proof that two records represent the same thing.

**Technical details and references.**

Choose the duplicate definition first: identical bytes, near-identical wording/pixels, or semantically similar content are different tasks. Exact hashing handles byte identity. MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity of shingles and LSH generates likely textual overlap candidates. SimHash approximates cosine similarity of weighted feature sets. Neural embeddings capture semantic similarity but may merge distinct documents discussing the same topic.

Use a candidate-generation stage followed by a stricter pairwise verification stage. For images use perceptual features robust to intended transforms; for video compare temporal frame/segment signatures rather than a single thumbnail. Store canonical IDs, versions, and deletion lineage, and retain reasons for merges so errors can be undone.

Tune thresholds on labeled pairs including hard nonduplicates and transformations. Avoid naive transitive closure when A resembles B and B resembles C but A does not resemble C. Evaluate precision/recall by duplicate type, cluster quality, throughput, and index freshness. Sharded LSH/ANN indexes improve scale but require careful handling of hot buckets and high-frequency boilerplate.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** MinHash collision probability equals Jaccard similarity of the represented sets; random-hyperplane sign agreement equals $1-\theta/\pi$ for angular similarity. These support candidate generation under different notions of similarity. Use stricter verification before merging records, and retain reversible cluster decisions because approximate similarity is not necessarily transitive. [3](https://nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book/)
